name: Murata-grm_GRM31CC81E226KE11
title: 22 µF 25 V X6S multilayer ceramic chip capacitor, 3216M (1206)
summary: GRM31CC81E226KE11 is a surface-mount multilayer ceramic capacitor of 22 µF ±10 % rated at 25 V DC, in a 3.2 × 1.6 × 1.6 mm (EIA 1206) body with an X6S class II dielectric. Its capacitance stays within ±22 % of the 25 °C value from -55 °C to 105 °C with no bias applied, and it may be reflow or flow soldered. It is intended for consumer and industrial equipment, medical equipment other than implants (GHTF A, B, C), and automotive infotainment and comfort equipment.

operation.text: The rated 25 V DC is the most that may sit across the terminals at any time. With AC on top of DC, the DC level plus the AC peak must stay within it; with pure AC or pulses, the peak-to-peak swing must. Surges, ESD and pulse spikes are held to the same limit. Overvoltage can break down the internal dielectric layers and short the part, after a time that depends on how high the voltage is and how hot the part runs.

AC or pulse current through the part warms it through dielectric loss, and the warmed surface must still stay within 105 °C. For parts rated below 100 V DC, the load is kept so that the body rises less than 20 °C above a 25 °C ambient. An example for a 10 µF 10 V R(R1) part shows the temperature rise climbing with ripple current at 100 kHz, 500 kHz and 1 MHz.

Capacitance of high-permittivity ceramic parts falls as DC voltage is applied, and falls faster the higher the voltage, even below the rating. In the example of a 0.1 µF 50 V X7R part, capacitance is about 10 % down at 20 V and about 50 % down at 50 V.

Capacitance also depends on the AC measuring or operating level. In the example of a 10 µF 6.3 V X7R part it is about 30 % below nominal at very low AC level and some 20 % above at 2 Vrms. Capacitance is measured at 120 Hz and 0.5 Vrms; at high capacitance a meter's output can sag, so the voltage really across the part should be confirmed.

The X6S characteristic holds capacitance within -22 % to +22 % of its 25 °C value from -55 °C to 105 °C without bias. In circuits that need a narrow capacitance tolerance, such as time-constant networks, the temperature characteristic is checked under the real operating conditions.

High-permittivity dielectrics lose capacitance with time. In the example curves a C0G part stays flat, an X7R part loses roughly 4 % and an X5R part roughly 9 % by about 3000 hours. In circuits that need a narrow tolerance, aging is weighed together with the voltage and temperature characteristics.
Under AC or pulse drive a high-permittivity capacitor vibrates at certain frequencies and may make audible noise; mechanical shock or vibration applied to it can also produce noise.

General-purpose GRM products are designed for equipment lasting about 10 years, and can exceed 10 years when held at 80 % of rated voltage or less and 20 °C below the maximum operating temperature. Products made for consumer equipment are designed for over 5 years under the same derating. Useful life means the time to 1 % cumulative failure in continuous use; the charts are estimates, not guarantees.

A capacitor cracked by a drop or board flex can lose insulation and short. Where a short could cause shock, smoke or fire, a fuse or other fail-safe is needed. This series carries no safety-standard certification.

Water, brine or condensation can short the part, corrode the terminations and shorten its life. Solvents and corrosive or volatile gases, over long exposure, oxidize the terminations and degrades insulation, up to breakdown. The part is kept away from oil and water spray, direct sunlight, ozone, ultraviolet light, radiation, toxic gases such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur dioxide, chlorine and ammonia, and vibration beyond its limits; damp-proofing is used where condensation can form.

Stock is kept at 5 to 40 °C (below 30 °C preferred) and 20 to 70 % relative humidity, away from sunlight, corrosive gas and sudden humidity changes, and used soon after delivery. After six months the packaging and mounting are checked; after a year the solderability too, since the electrodes can oxidize.

Chip parts take board flex directly, and a tall solder fillet multiplies the stress, so lands are sized to keep fillets low. A board whose thermal expansion differs strongly from the ceramic, such as fluororesin or single-layer glass epoxy, can crack the chip through heating cycles. Moving to a smaller case means revisiting land size, trace width and direction and copper thickness, not just the land. Solder resist separates the chip's solder from a nearby chassis, from a leaded part's lead and between side-by-side chips.

The chip is turned so that its long axis lies across the direction in which the board bends. Near a board separation line, stress is reduced by turning the chip parallel to the line, cutting slits in the separation part and keeping the chip away from the line; all three together work best.

Bending or twisting a populated board can crack the capacitor and lead to an insulation fault or short. A router-type separator is preferred; a jig or disc separator needs aligned blades and a correct V-groove angle and depth; hand and nipper separation stress the board too much. With a jig on a single-sided board, the board is held near the jig and bent toward the side carrying the capacitors.

The pick-up nozzle's lowest point is set so it does not bend the board, with support beneath. Worn locating claws and dirty nozzles push unevenly and crack chips, so both are serviced and replaced regularly. The same care applies when parts are placed on the second side, when leaded parts are inserted, when connectors are mated and when screws are tightened.

Components and board are preheated so that the solder-to-component difference stays within 190 °C for this case size, and the same limit applies when the hot board goes into solvent. Peak is 240 to 260 °C with Sn-3.0Ag-0.5Cu in air or nitrogen. A peak below the one the solder supplier specifies risks poor wetting, voids, whiskers, weak joints, poor self-alignment, tombstoning and shifting. Too much paste makes a tall fillet that cracks under stress; too little leaves a weak joint.

The 31 case may be flow soldered with a temperature difference within 150 °C. Preheat peaks at 100 to 120 °C and the solder at 250 to 260 °C. Overlong or overhot soldering leaches the terminations and can lose contact to the inner electrodes, reducing capacitance. The fillet top stays below the chip's thickness. Where the chip is first fixed with adhesive, the adhesive is epoxy with good strength, wet strength, insulation, pot life and fast cure, non-corrosive and halogen-free, applied between the lands under the chip.

Rework starts with preheating the chip and board to at least 150 °C and finishes without rapid cooling. The iron tip is no hotter than 350 °C, no more than 3 mm across, and applied briefly; solder wire is 0.5 mm or finer, and the iron does not touch the chip. A spot heater is kept 5 mm or more away, at 45°, with outlet air at 400 °C max., for under 10 s on chips of 3.2 × 1.6 mm or smaller.

Strong ultrasonic cleaning can resonate the board and crack chips or joints, so the cleaning process is qualified first; flux residue left behind degrades the part. Strongly acidic flux corrodes it. A coating resin with low cure shrinkage, low moisture absorption and thermal expansion close to the ceramic is chosen; silicone can be used as a stress-buffering undercoat and epoxy as a low-absorption coat. Strongly acidic coatings are avoided.
Test probes can flex the board and crack chips or joints, so support pins are placed under the board close to each probe, and the probe contact is made without shock.

A dropped capacitor or dropped board is not used. Populated boards are held at the edges with both hands, and board corners are kept from striking chips when boards are stacked. Parts removed from equipment are not reused. Sn-Zn solder degrades MLCC reliability.
